ruling: - **R26. Batches stop wasting CI.** Owner 09:20 CST Nov 11: "i need a review and then a strategy that makes me parallelize as much as possible, without losing time when things start merging into main". And 09:21 CST: "batch merges themselves were made to avoid CI waits and to have things go faster". In the question box, answered by 10:00 CST, he picked these parts. 1. A lane's own checks run what made batches red: the Windows slice, mutation tests on the files it touches, and signed-commit cases (folds into 3.5). 2. A lane dropped from two batches leaves the queue for a fix lane. 3. No self-made reruns: the merge tool stops the records-page push after a green run, and a red main is fixed before the next merge, not waited out. 4. Busy files in turn (box answer 10:05 CST, "Both"). The batch runner puts lanes that touch the same busy file (the main guard file, its tests, its mutation tests) into back-to-back stacked batches, never one batch. The guard test file is split into one file per rule. The split runs first in stage 3, while few lanes are open. Stays as ruled: decision batch-freeze-lane-set (owner 2026-11-08 20:24 and 20:31 CST): the set freezes at build, the next batch stacks on the running one, a red run drops only the blamed lane. Its tool check is this item's step. One batch runner: merging is one at a time under one lock (merge.py). Evidence (audit 09:37 CST, last 15 batch merges, 256 lanes): 3030 CI minutes, 677 on merged heads. 74 builds became 15 merges, with 147 lane drops; two lanes were dropped in 5+ batches each. Lane wait, last commit to merge, has a median of 536 min, 397 of it before the build. A lone CI run takes 33-38 min (5 runs). Merge queue: GitHub offers it to organization repos only.
